results.name: set_level_heterogeneity
results.description: Standard deviation, across example sets with at least 20 non-example trials, of each set's non-example yes-rate; observed above the null means sets differ more in overall generalization breadth (some diffuse, some tight) than the model reproduces, below means the model exaggerates between-set differences.

# name: set_level_heterogeneity
# description: Standard deviation, across example sets with at least 20 non-example trials, of each set's non-example yes-rate; observed above the null means sets differ more in overall generalization breadth (some diffuse, some tight) than the model reproduces, below means the model exaggerates between-set differences.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).reindex(columns=range(4)).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)
    Dg = np.where(np.isnan(E), np.nan, np.mod(E, 10))
    is_ex = np.any(E == t[:, None], axis=1)
    g = pd.DataFrame({"s": df["number_set"].astype(str).to_numpy()[~is_ex], "r": r[~is_ex]}).groupby("s")["r"].agg(["mean", "size"])
    g = g[g["size"] >= 20]
    if len(g) < 2:
        return 0.0
    return float(g["mean"].std())

results.name: range_edge_asymmetry
results.description: In 2-4 example sets, among non-example targets sharing no final digit with any example, yes-rate for targets 1-10 above the largest example minus targets 1-10 below the smallest example; observed above the null means people extend ranges upward more (relative to downward) than the model's compressed number line predicts, below means the model's upward bias is too strong or people favour smaller numbers.
results.code:
# name: range_edge_asymmetry
# description: In 2-4 example sets, among non-example targets sharing no final digit with any example, yes-rate for targets 1-10 above the largest example minus targets 1-10 below the smallest example; observed above the null means people extend ranges upward more (relative to downward) than the model's compressed number line predicts, below means the model's upward bias is too strong or people favour smaller numbers.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).reindex(columns=range(4)).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)
    Dg = np.where(np.isnan(E), np.nan, np.mod(E, 10))
    is_ex = np.any(E == t[:, None], axis=1)
    mn = np.nanmin(E, axis=1)
    mx = np.nanmax(E, axis=1)
    nondig = ~is_ex & ~np.any(Dg == np.mod(t, 10)[:, None], axis=1)
    a = (n >= 2) & nondig & (t > mx) & (t - mx <= 10)
    b = (n >= 2) & nondig & (t < mn) & (mn - t <= 10)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: parity_far_generalization
results.description: In 2-4 example sets whose examples all share a parity, yes-rate for same-parity non-example targets more than 10 from every example and sharing no final digit with any example, minus the yes-rate for opposite-parity targets meeting the same conditions; observed above the null means people extend a parity rule to distant numbers more than the model, below means the model's parity generalization is too strong.
results.code:
# name: parity_far_generalization
# description: In 2-4 example sets whose examples all share a parity, yes-rate for same-parity non-example targets more than 10 from every example and sharing no final digit with any example, minus the yes-rate for opposite-parity targets meeting the same conditions; observed above the null means people extend a parity rule to distant numbers more than the model, below means the model's parity generalization is too strong.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).reindex(columns=range(4)).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)
    Dg = np.where(np.isnan(E), np.nan, np.mod(E, 10))
    is_ex = np.any(E == t[:, None], axis=1)
    dist = np.nanmin(np.abs(E - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    par = np.where(np.isnan(E), np.nan, np.mod(E, 2))
    odd_n = np.nansum(par == 1, axis=1)
    even_n = np.nansum(par == 0, axis=1)
    allp = (n >= 2) & ((odd_n == n) | (even_n == n))
    set_par = np.where(odd_n == n, 1, 0)
    nondig = ~is_ex & ~np.any(Dg == np.mod(t, 10)[:, None], axis=1)
    base = allp & nondig & (dist > 10)
    a = base & (np.mod(t, 2) == set_par)
    b = base & (np.mod(t, 2) != set_par)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: math_rule_consistent_targets
results.description: In 2-4 example sets, yes-rate for non-example targets that share no final digit with any example but belong to a mathematical rule (squares, cubes, powers of 2-10, multiples of 3-12) containing every example; observed above the null means people endorse such rule-consistent numbers more than the model, below means the model over-weights these mathematical rules.
results.code:
# name: math_rule_consistent_targets
# description: In 2-4 example sets, yes-rate for non-example targets that share no final digit with any example but belong to a mathematical rule (squares, cubes, powers of 2-10, multiples of 3-12) containing every example; observed above the null means people endorse such rule-consistent numbers more than the model, below means the model over-weights these mathematical rules.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).reindex(columns=range(4)).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)
    Dg = np.where(np.isnan(E), np.nan, np.mod(E, 10))
    is_ex = np.any(E == t[:, None], axis=1)
    nums = np.arange(1, 101)
    rules = [[k * k for k in range(1, 11)], [k ** 3 for k in range(1, 5)]]
    rules += [[m ** k for k in range(1, 8) if m ** k <= 100] for m in range(2, 11)]
    rules += [list(range(m, 101, m)) for m in [3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 11, 12]]
    M = np.array([np.isin(nums, c) for c in rules])  # (R, 100)
    Ei = np.where(np.isnan(E), 1, E).astype(int) - 1
    memb = M[:, Ei]  # (R, rows, 4)
    memb = memb | np.isnan(E)[None, :, :]
    consistent = memb.all(axis=2)  # (R, rows)
    ti = np.clip(t.astype(int), 1, 100) - 1
    t_in = M[:, ti]  # (R, rows)
    hit = np.any(consistent & t_in, axis=0)
    nondig = ~is_ex & ~np.any(Dg == np.mod(t, 10)[:, None], axis=1)
    a = (n >= 2) & nondig & hit
    if a.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean())

results.name: decade_boundary_effect
results.description: In 2-4 example sets, among non-example targets whose final digit matches no example and whose distance to the nearest example is 4-9, yes-rate for targets sharing a tens digit (decade) with some example minus those sharing none; observed above the null means people use decade membership beyond numeric distance more than the model (rules + intervals) predicts, below means the model over-produces a decade effect.
results.code:
# name: decade_boundary_effect
# description: In 2-4 example sets, among non-example targets whose final digit matches no example and whose distance to the nearest example is 4-9, yes-rate for targets sharing a tens digit (decade) with some example minus those sharing none; observed above the null means people use decade membership beyond numeric distance more than the model (rules + intervals) predicts, below means the model over-produces a decade effect.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).reindex(columns=range(4)).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)
    Dg = np.where(np.isnan(E), np.nan, np.mod(E, 10))
    is_ex = np.any(E == t[:, None], axis=1)
    dist = np.nanmin(np.abs(E - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    nondig = ~is_ex & ~np.any(Dg == np.mod(t, 10)[:, None], axis=1)
    dec = np.any(np.floor(E / 10) == np.floor(t / 10)[:, None], axis=1)
    base = (n >= 2) & nondig & (dist >= 4) & (dist <= 9)
    a = base & dec
    b = base & ~dec
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: outlier_neighbourhood_falloff
results.description: In 3-4 example sets where all but one example share a final digit, yes-rate for off-majority-digit non-example targets at distance 1 from the outlier example minus at distance 2-3; the model's radius prior (smaller radii likelier) predicts a positive falloff, so observed below the null means people endorse the outlier's neighbourhood more uniformly (flatter) than the model, above means a steeper falloff.
results.code:
# name: outlier_neighbourhood_falloff
# description: In 3-4 example sets where all but one example share a final digit, yes-rate for off-majority-digit non-example targets at distance 1 from the outlier example minus at distance 2-3; the model's radius prior (smaller radii likelier) predicts a positive falloff, so observed below the null means people endorse the outlier's neighbourhood more uniformly (flatter) than the model, above means a steeper falloff.
def test_statistic(df):
    E = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).reindex(columns=range(4)).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(E), axis=1)
    Dg = np.where(np.isnan(E), np.nan, np.mod(E, 10))
    is_ex = np.any(E == t[:, None], axis=1)
    same = np.sum(Dg[:, :, None] == Dg[:, None, :], axis=2).astype(float)
    same[np.isnan(Dg)] = np.nan
    s0 = np.nan_to_num(same, nan=0)
    is_out = (same == 1) & ((s0 == 1).sum(axis=1)[:, None] == 1) & (np.nanmax(same, axis=1)[:, None] == (n - 1)[:, None])
    valid = (n >= 3) & is_out.any(axis=1)
    out_val = np.where(valid, np.nansum(np.where(is_out, E, 0.0), axis=1), np.nan)
    maj_digit = np.nansum(np.where(~is_out & ~np.isnan(E), Dg, 0.0), axis=1) / np.maximum(n - 1, 1)
    d_out = np.abs(t - out_val)
    off = valid & (np.mod(t, 10) != maj_digit) & ~is_ex
    a = off & (d_out == 1)
    b = off & (d_out >= 2) & (d_out <= 3)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: outlier_example_endorsement
results.description: In 3-4 example sets where all but one example share a final digit, yes-rate when the target is the outlier example itself; observed below the null means people reject the off-pattern example more often than the model (which treats it as a near-certain member via the exception channel/noise), above means they accept it more.

# name: outlier_example_endorsement
# description: In 3-4 example sets where all but one example share a final digit, yes-rate when the target is the outlier example itself; observed below the null means people reject the off-pattern example more often than the model (which treats it as a near-certain member via the exception channel/noise), above means they accept it more.
def test_statistic(df):

    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()

    Dg = np.where(np.isnan(E), np.nan, np.mod(E, 10))
    is_ex = np.any(E == t[:, None], axis=1)
    same = np.sum(Dg[:, :, None] == Dg[:, None, :], axis=2).astype(float)
    same[np.isnan(Dg)] = np.nan
    s0 = np.nan_to_num(same, nan=0)
    is_out = (same == 1) & ((s0 == 1).sum(axis=1)[:, None] == 1) & (np.nanmax(same, axis=1)[:, None] == (n - 1)[:, None])
    valid = (n >= 3) & is_out.any(axis=1)

    d_out = np.abs(t - out_val)

    a = valid & (t == out_val)
